nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: VLANs: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VLAN logically segments a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains. VLAN 10 traffic can't see VLAN 20 traffic without a Layer-3 routed hop, even on the same switch. This is the foundation of multi-tenant networking on shared hardware.

flashcards.front: Access port vs trunk port — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and strips the tag — end hosts don't see VLAN headers. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches using 802.1Q tags. Hosts plug into access ports; switches connect to each other via trunks.

flashcards.front: What is the native VLAN on a trunk?
flashcards.back: The native VLAN is the one VLAN that's NOT tagged on a trunk — frames in that VLAN traverse the link with no 802.1Q header. Defaults to VLAN 1 but should be changed to an unused VLAN on every trunk for security (prevents VLAN hopping attacks).

flashcards.front: Why use a Layer-3 SVI?
flashcards.back: A Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) gives a VLAN a Layer-3 address inside the switch — it's the inter-VLAN router. Without an SVI (or external router), VLANs can't talk to each other. Modern switches do inter-VLAN routing in hardware at wire speed.

flashcards.front: What's VLAN hopping?
flashcards.back: An attacker tricks the switch into forwarding their traffic into a VLAN they shouldn't be in. Two flavors: double-tagging (exploits the native-VLAN-untagged rule) and switch-spoofing (the host negotiates a trunk via DTP). Mitigation: tag the native VLAN, set ports to access mode explicitly, disable DTP.

nodes.title: Spanning Tree Protocol: Key Ideas
nodes.content: STP prevents loops on Ethernet networks by blocking redundant links. Without it, a single redundant cable between two switches creates a broadcast storm that takes the LAN down. STP automatically picks one root bridge and computes a loop-free tree.

flashcards.front: Why is loop prevention needed on Ethernet?
flashcards.back: Ethernet frames have no TTL — once a broadcast frame enters a loop it circulates forever, doubling on every pass, until the LAN melts. STP detects redundant paths and blocks them, leaving a spanning tree. If the active link fails, STP unblocks an alternate.

flashcards.front: How is the root bridge elected?
flashcards.back: Lowest bridge ID wins. Bridge ID = priority (default 32768, lower is better) followed by MAC address. In practice you set the priority on your core switches so root election is predictable, not whoever happens to have the lowest MAC.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between RSTP and classic STP?
flashcards.back: Classic 802.1D converges in 30-50 seconds (listen → learn → forward). RSTP (802.1w) converges in 1-2 seconds by negotiating port roles between adjacent switches instead of timing them out. Always use RSTP — classic STP is too slow for modern data centers.

flashcards.front: Portfast / Bridge Assurance — when do you enable them?
flashcards.back: PortFast bypasses the listening/learning states on access ports (anywhere an end host plugs in) — link comes up forwarding immediately. NEVER enable PortFast on a switch-to-switch trunk; it lets loops form during reconvergence.

nodes.title: Fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Fundamentals. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An IPv4 /26 subnet has 26 bits of network and 6 bits of host. The host range minus the network address minus the broadcast address gives the number of USABLE host addresses on that subnet. How many?
flashcards.back: /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 total addresses. Subtract 1 network + 1 broadcast = 62 usable hosts.

flashcards.front: An IPv4 subnet is defined with prefix length /28 (28 bits used for the network portion). In dotted-decimal form, what does the matching subnet mask look like?
flashcards.back: /28 sets 28 bits to 1. The last octet: 11110000 = 240. So the mask is 255.255.255.240.

flashcards.front: An interface is configured with `ip address 192.168.1.64 255.255.255.192` (i.e. 192.168.1.64/26). What is the directed broadcast address for this subnet?
flashcards.back: /26 = 64 addresses per subnet. Starting at .64, the range ends at .127. The broadcast is 192.168.1.127.

flashcards.front: Gi0/1 on a switch is connected via a UTP cable to a server's NIC, both sides locked to 1000/full. The link has been up for 24 hours. The interface counters show ZERO collisions, ZERO late collisions, and ZERO CSMA/CD-related events. Why are there no collisions on this link?
flashcards.back: Full-duplex uses separate TX and RX wires, eliminating collisions entirely. CSMA/CD is disabled in full-duplex mode. Half-duplex shares the medium and uses CSMA/CD.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.
